newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Price key to any Russia grain buys - Zaveruykha aide.
newsitem.headline: Price key to any Russia grain buys - Zaveruykha aide.

text.p: Price is the main determining factor that would motivate Russian grain imports, an aide to a senior cabinet official said on Thursday.

Nikolai Dolgushkin, aide to Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Zaveryukha, in charge of the harvest, repeated statements by Russian officials that Russia could possibly import Australian, Canadian or U.S. wheat to its Far East port of Vladivostok.
"I don't know from whom we might do this -- there's Canada, Australia and the United States," he said. "Cheshinsky would take the cheapest offer."

Zaveryukha said on Wednesday that Leonid Cheshinsky, president of semi-state grain buying agency Roskhleboprodukt, would hold talks on Thursday with Canadian grain representatives in town for a Russian-Canadian economic summit.
Representatives of the Canadian Wheat Board, which has a monopoly on Canadian wheat and barley exports, are part of the delegation to Moscow.
A Roskhleboprodukt source said that as far as he knew no deals had been reached. Cheshinsky and Canadian embassy officials in Moscow declined to comment.

"We have enough wheat," said Dolgushkin, adding nonetheless that it would be cheaper for Russia to import for its far-flung regions than to drag domestic grain thousands of km (miles) across the country at expensive rail tariff rates.
One Moscow trade source said he thought the Russians could source to Canada or Australia, both with bumper crops, and not to the United States, where stocks are at 20-year lows.
Agriculture Minister Viktor Khlystun has said Russia may buy 500,000 tonnes of food wheat from North America or Australia.
Dolgushkin said it was likely that Russia would try to raise money by selling some of its own grain to ex-Soviet neighbours.
A Roskhleboprodukt source said earlier this month the agency was seeking state approval to barter 400,000 tonnes of domestic grain to Uzbekistan for an unspecified amount of cotton.
Russia is eyeing its second bad harvest in a row of around 70 million tonnes net and has virtually no carryover stocks. --Lynnley Browning, Moscow Newsroom, +7095 941 8520
